SASRec combines item and learned positional embeddings; deletion therefore changes both available evidence and potentially surviving events’ positions. Its original positional-embedding ablation helped sparse Beauty data but hurt denser datasets, showing that position effects depend on the dataset ([SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781)). Counterfactual recommendation research uses history deletion to measure recommendation dependence, but dependence alone does not establish harmful behavior ([Learning to Counterfactually Explain Recommendations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09752)).

Recommended diagnostic design, inferred from these mechanisms: compare compacted deletion against position-preserving masking of exactly the same events. Compaction removes events and repacks survivors; masking retains survivors’ original position IDs and blocks removed slots as attention keys/values. Padding IDs alone may not implement this correctly. Both interventions reduce visible context; their difference indicates sensitivity to repacking and positions, including interactions with content. Compare targeted deletion with repeated random deletions matched by count and event age/recency, within the same histories. Keep the last observed item and prediction position fixed in every arm to control immediate-transition evidence and readout changes. Effects persisting under masking and exceeding matched-random effects support event-specific dependence, without proving real-world causality; masking itself can create unfamiliar inputs.

Link dependence to accuracy using paired validation measurements with identical users, targets, and pinned candidates: target-rank changes, HR@10 gains/losses, and category-macro ΔHR@10. Score shifts or recommendation turnover alone cannot identify harm. Improved target ranking after targeted removal, beyond matched-random removal and consistent across position controls, supports harmful dependence; deterioration supports useful historical evidence. Report uncertainty and results by history length/category. These are proposed controls, not measured findings on the four RecHarness datasets.
